concept.name: Preferred stock
concept.definition: A class of stock whose holders usually do not have voting rights but receive dividend payments before common stockholders and have priority over common stockholders if the company goes bankrupt and its assets are liquidated. Dividends are typically set at a fixed rate on a stated par value.
concept.intuition: Preferred stock trades away voting power and unlimited upside for a senior, more bond-like income stream.
concept.mechanics: Preferreds pay a stated dividend that may be cumulative (missed payments accrue and must be paid before common dividends) or non-cumulative. Issues are often callable by the issuer and sometimes convertible into common stock; in the capital structure they rank below all debt but above common equity.
concept.failure_modes: Dividends can be suspended (in non-cumulative issues, skipped payments are lost), and fixed-rate preferreds behave like long-duration bonds, falling when interest rates rise. Holders have no vote to influence management and rank behind every creditor in distress.
concept.misconceptions: That 'preferred' means safer than bonds — preferreds are junior to all debt and their dividends are discretionary. Also, the fixed dividend is not an interest obligation, so skipping it is not a default.
concept.example: A $25 par preferred with a 6% rate pays $1.50 per year, and that dividend must be paid in full before any common stock dividend can be declared.
